title: Service request intake and classification
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Any worker in any home-service business, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for service request intake and classification and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for service request intake and classification under company and local requirements.

instruction.heading: Why intake comes first
instruction.body: Every request starts as a claim about work, and the first decision is whether your business should accept that work at all. Intake is the point where a request is written down, understood and sorted before any quote is given or any equipment is loaded. A request that looks routine can hide unidentified materials, access limits or a need for a licence, so classify it on evidence and not on how familiar it sounds. This lesson covers how to collect the facts, how to sort the request into one of four outcomes, and how to record the decision so that the next person can see why it was made.

instruction.heading: Collect the facts before you classify
instruction.body: Obtain the request in writing where you can. Record the site address, the named site contact, the person who can approve the work, the expected result in the client's own words, and any materials, products or equipment the client expects you to use. Ask about access and occupancy: who is on the premises, whether children, animals or people with health conditions are present, which areas are restricted, and when the site can be entered. Keep what you have observed separate from what someone has told you and from what is still unknown. Photographs taken within safe access help the record, but a photograph does not identify an unknown substance or confirm that a surface or structure is safe. A client's statement that something is harmless or routine is not proof.

instruction.heading: Classify the request into one outcome
instruction.body: Once the facts are gathered, place the request in one of four outcomes. Accept means the work sits within the worker's documented training, the business's approved methods and products, and the authority the site has given. Accept with controls means the work is in scope once named controls, such as ventilation, an exclusion zone or a second worker, are in place. Hold means facts or authority are missing, so no work starts until they arrive. Refer means the work involves a licensed trade, a regulated material, a specialist method or a risk the business is not competent to manage, so it goes to an appropriately authorised provider. A quote given during intake is not work permission, and a hold or refer outcome must be stated in both the quote and the job record.

instruction.heading: Worked decision on an unidentified residue
instruction.body: Suppose an office manager asks for removal of a dark residue on office carpet, and nobody knows what it is or how it got there. The request cannot be classified as routine cleaning. The correct classification is uncharacterised: the material is not identified, its hazard is not known, and the client's wish to have it removed does not change that. The response is to request photographs, the product history, any cleaning records, the building's access rules and a qualified inspection. The cleaner does not label the residue, does not test it with cleaning products, and does not promise that it will come out. The client is told why the job is on hold, and the named approver is recorded.

instruction.heading: Record the decision and the restart conditions
instruction.body: Record the classification, the scope and any exclusions, the controls required, the decision (accept, accept with controls, hold or refer), the person who approved it and the date. Keep a copy of what the client was told. Before work restarts, confirm who can restart it, which control check must be completed, and which documents must travel with the job. If a risk stays unresolved, escalate it to a competent specialist rather than closing the intake record.

instruction.heading: Licence notice
instruction.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, permit or authority to do any work. Some tasks that appear in a service request need a licence, a permit or a specific authorisation in some states and territories. Completing this lesson does not make a worker competent or authorised for any regulated task.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before resuming if the scope is unclear, if a hazard is identified or suspected and not yet understood, if the request calls for work outside your training or the work order, if the client asks you to start before authority is confirmed, or if people or animals enter the area while work is in progress.

procedure: Record the request in writing, with the site, the named contact, the person who can approve the work and the expected result in the client's words.
Ask about access, occupancy, children, animals and restricted areas, and record when the site can be entered.
Separate what you have observed from what others have reported and from what remains unknown.
Identify the materials, products, equipment and hazards the request involves, and mark any unidentified material as uncharacterised.
Compare the request with your training, your employer's authorisation, the approved methods and any licence rules that apply, and record the gap.
Choose one outcome (accept, accept with controls, hold or refer) and name the person who approves it.
Tell the client the outcome in plain language, without assurances the evidence does not support.
Record the decision, the exclusions, the controls and the restart conditions in the job record.

workedExamples.situation: An office manager requests removal of an unidentified dark residue on carpet.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first safe action is to stop short of any treatment and classify the job as uncharacterised. Do not test the residue with cleaning products and do not promise removal. Ask for photographs, the product history, the cause if known, the building's access rules and a qualified inspection. Tell the office manager that the job is on hold and why, and record the named approver who will decide whether and how work proceeds.

workedExamples.situation: An office manager requests an unspecified specialist clean of an area with unknown stains and odours.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the job be accepted as a routine clean?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The request does not state the method, the material or the result, and the stains and odours are unknown, so the job cannot be classified as routine. Record the outcome as hold. Ask for the specific area, the stain and odour history, the expected result and any product or method the client has in mind. Arrange an inspection by someone with the right competence before any quote is treated as a commitment. If the inspection finds a regulated or hazardous material, the job is referred.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence notice: completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated or restricted work. Check the licence or authorisation rules for your state or territory, and obtain your employer or site written authorisation before starting any work that is outside your training.

Stop-work rule: stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before continuing if the task is outside your training or authorisation, the hazard or the required permission is unclear, or the client asks for work that the work order does not cover.

qualityStandard: The request is classified on evidence (accept, accept with controls, hold or refer) before any quote is given or equipment is loaded.
Missing facts are a reason to hold the job, and what was observed, what was reported and what is unknown are kept apart.
The decision names the approver, the exclusions, the controls and the restart conditions, and is recorded in the job record.
Uncharacterised material is not labelled, tested with cleaning products or promised to be removed.
summary: Classify each request on evidence before accepting it, and treat missing facts as a reason to hold the job.
Keep what you observed, what others reported and what remains unknown in separate parts of the record.
Use four outcomes: accept, accept with controls, hold or refer.
A quote is not permission to work, and a client's assurance is not proof of safety.
Record the approver, the exclusions, the controls and the restart conditions so the decision can be traced.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before starting work classified as "Service request intake and classification", what must you do?
options: Start the work and check hazards as you go, since the client has asked for it and the client has paid a deposit
Identify task-specific unknown hazards, qualifications, permissions and controls; place work on hold until verified.
Accept the task if your past experience with similar jobs was safe and the client has been clear about what they want
Ask the client to sign a waiver so the work can begin and the waiver covers every hazard on site

knowledgeChecks.question: Can an intake request for restricted work be accepted on a training certificate alone?
options: Yes, a training certificate alone covers the basic permit and the client has agreed to the job
Yes, if the client agrees in writing and the client pays a deposit up front for the job
No. Relevant licences, employer/site authorisation and independent competence verification remain required.
Only if the work is outdoors and at ground level and the work is short, simple and low risk

knowledgeChecks.question: Before classifying a request, what does the lesson say to collect?
options: Only the price the client expects
The facts: the site address, the named site contact, the person who can approve, and the expected result in the client's own words
A waiver signed by the client
